summary: The article examines the proposed golf ball rollback policy from the R&A and USGA, which aims to curb the distance balls travel to avoid endlessly lengthening courses. The rules are non-binding, so tours could reject them and create a split between amateur and pro equipment. It surveys reactions from players, including opposition from Justin Thomas and Bryson DeChambeau and support from Rory McIlroy and Tiger Woods, and considers the effect on majors and LIV Golf.
one_line: The R&A and USGA's proposed golf ball rollback is non-binding and divisive, drawing mixed reactions from pros and raising questions about majors, the PGA Tour and LIV Golf.
key_facts: The R&A and USGA decided to bring in a golf ball rollback policy because new technologies mean balls travel much farther, lengthening courses and burdening clubs financially.
The R&A and USGA organize 35 championships between themselves.
The rules are non-binding, so tours and regional governing bodies can decide for themselves whether to implement them; the proposed rules are not set to be implemented before at least 2026.
If passed, the limited-flight balls would be used in The Open (R&A) and the U.S. Open (USGA); Augusta National and PGA of America decide for the other majors.
Seth Waugh, the PGA of America CEO, denounced the proposals in a memo to the R&A, taking along nine other PGAs across the globe.
Fred Ridley, chairman of Augusta National, did not bang the drum for the rule but said he would much prefer to see the issue finally addressed.

The rules will apply only to men's golf, because the LPGA Tour's average driving distance is still within the accepted norm of the two governing bodies, even though Lexi Thompson shot a 316-yard drive at the Shrines Children's Open.
Justin Thomas, a fifteen-time Tour winner and PGA Tour policy board member, called the USGA's decisions "selfish" and compared the issue to the NBA hoop staying at 10 feet.
Bryson DeChambeau, who joined LIV Golf in 2022, called the policy "atrocious" and regularly hits drives of 310–320 yards.
Rory McIlroy, who leads the PGA Tour in driving distance at 326.7 yards, backed the proposal for elite golfers, saying it would make players hit long and mid irons again.
Tiger Woods said "this should have happened a long time ago" and that pros should play a pro ball while amateurs use an amateur ball.
As of this year, 28 of 48 LIV golfers average over 300 yards driving distance, with Dustin Johnson and DeChambeau in the top five.
